perfil_profesional: I am a medical doctor and doctorate in biomedical sciences from the National University of Colombia. I currently coordinate the physiology unit at U del Rosario. My work focuses on understanding blood donation processes, safety for blood donors and recipients, as well as the proper use of blood components and transfusion alternatives.

proyectos: Tipo de proyecto: Investigación y desarrollo ClC channels/transporters as potential therapeutic targets against Leishmania. DAAD support Inicio: Abril 2013 Fin: Junio 2013 Duración Resumen Leishmaniasis is s common tropical diseases infecting 12 million people worldwide but being a risk for 350 million more. Despite its prevalence, this disease is under-represented in basic biological research. Therefore, it is imperative to investigate the molecular and physiological mechanisms underlying the parasitic nature of this protozoan as well as the mechanisms involved in ionic homeostasis that support parasite survival. Leishmaniasis is caused by parasites of the genus Leishmania, which comprise two stages that develop between an invertebrate and a vertebrate. A free form is found in the gut of the mosquito vector, the promastigote, and an intracellular form in the vertebrate host, the amastigote. In the gut the parasite is extracellular in close contact with the intestine cells and expose to fluctuations in osmolarity, nutrient availability and an alkaline pH. Within their host cell in the vertebrate, Leishmania is confined to a phagolysosomal compartment, the parasitophorous vacuole (PV), which is acidic and rich in proteolytic enzymes. Parasite adaptation to these environments requires expression of molecules such as ion channels, particularly shunt chloride currents associated with pump functioning and nutrient transport. We have described chloride currents in oocytes injected with Leishmania mRNA, and started the studies on a family of ion channels that may explain these currents. The aim of this project is the electrophysiological characterization of this family of ClC channels/transporters of Leishmania as a step in the understanding of functional importance in parasite survival of these molecules.
